newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN wants oil monitors to go to Iraq soon.
newsitem.headline: UN wants oil monitors to go to Iraq soon.

text.p: A U.N. official said on Tuesday he was trying to get visas for three oil monitors from the Dutch-based Saybolt firm to go to Iraq soon, even if the oil-for-food plan is delayed.
But he said sending monitors for the distribution of food and other supplies would be "down the road" a bit.
The official, Under Secrtetary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan made the comments after he told reporters that minimum conditions do not exist yet in northern Iraq to implement the oil-for-food plan.

"We are trying to move on whatever front it is possible to move," he told reporters. "We have asked the Saybolt company to send an advance team of three to go there as soon as possible and as soon as they get the visas. These experts will inspect the oil installations and metering stations. they will also discuss other related matters."

Gharekhan, in answer to questions, said that the lack of agreement in the Security Council's sanctions committee on an oil pricing formula would not prevent oil contracts from being approved once the U.N. decided the plan had to be implemented.
He said the committee, if necessary, could approve the contracts on an individual basis, indicating the sanctions committee's procedures were not holding up the deal.

A senior Security Council source said he believed that there would be no movement on the oil-for-food planl until after the November 5 U.S. election, saying that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali did not want to see this agreement made a football in the campaign.

A U.S. official said earlier he also believed there were too many Iraqi intelligence officials in the north and that they could impede the distribution of food by watching what any Kurds involved in the operation were doing.

The oil-for-food deal was signed between Iraq and the United Nations on May 2 and allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy badly needed food, medicine and other humanitarian goods.

It was about to be implemented early in September when President Saddam Hussein sent his troops to the Kurdish areas to help one feuding Kurdish faction and the United States responded with missile attacks. Boutros-Ghali then put the plan on hold.
